title: readonly struct and in
sub: Defensive copies you can't see in the code
cards/0/body:
Pass a struct to a method and it gets copied. For a small one (int, Point) that is cheap. A 4×4 matrix is already 64 bytes on every call.

ref and in pass a reference instead of a copy. in also promises that the method won't change the struct.
cards/1/task: Get rid of the matrix copies, but make sure the method can't mess up the caller's matrix.
cards/2/q: Why did copies remain with in but without readonly struct?
cards/2/options/0: The compiler doesn't know whether Det() and Trace() change the struct, so it calls them on a copy to keep the in promise
cards/2/explain: That is a defensive copy: invisible, but real.
cards/3/task: This one already uses in, yet there are two copies per call. Remove them without changing how the matrix is passed.
cards/4/body:
readonly struct promises that no method changes the fields. The compiler checks this and can then call methods directly on the original — even through in.

In a regular struct you can mark individual methods readonly.
cards/5/q: What is the danger of ref instead of in?
cards/5/options/0: The method can change the caller's struct
cards/5/explain: ref is for when you actually want the change.
cards/6/q: Match the passing mode to its behavior
cards/7/explain: The pair that in was invented for.
cards/8/q: A Point struct holds two ints. Is it worth passing it with in?
cards/8/options/0: Usually not: copying 8 bytes costs no more than passing a reference
cards/8/explain: in pays off for large structs — 16–32 bytes and up.
